fuentes/calendario-de-coligny/resumen.texto: Bronze plaque measuring 1.35 by 0.78 meters, found in 1897 at Coligny (Ain) in 73 fragments that preserve about 40% of the original. It is a five-year lunisolar calendar, with months of 29 or 30 days divided into two fortnights, two intercalary months, and marks for auspicious (MAT) and inauspicious (ANM) days. The first month is Samonios, and on it appears the annotation TRINOX SAMONI SINDIV, “three nights of Samonios today”. Judging by the lettering and the statue found with it, it is dated to the late 2nd century, but copying errors show that the reckoning is older. Fragments of another identical calendar came out at the sanctuary of Villards-d'Héria (Jura).

fuentes/calendario-de-coligny/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the longest inscriptions in Gaulish and the only direct proof that the Gauls had their own reckoning of time, as Caesar says (BG VI.18: they reckon time by nights) and Pliny also says (the druids begin months and years on the sixth day of the moon). It is debated whether Samonios marked the beginning of summer or of winter, and whether its name is the same as that of the Irish Samain; full reconstructions, such as Garrett Olmsted's, are hypotheses.

fuentes/tablilla-de-larzac/resumen.texto: Lead tablet broken into two pieces, found in 1983 in a grave in the La Vayssière necropolis, at L'Hospitalet-du-Larzac (Aveyron), and dated to around the year 100. With more than a thousand letters and about 160 words, it is the longest continuous text in Gaulish. It is a curse written in the “world of women”: it names several women, apparently two rival groups of sorceresses, and uses the expression bnanom brictom, “women's magic”. Its translation remains uncertain.

fuentes/tablilla-de-larzac/por_que_impor.texto: Together with the one from Chamalières, it shows that in Roman Gaul ritual magic of the same kind as Greco-Roman curses was written in Gaulish, and that the grave served as a route to the gods below. It was published by Michel Lejeune, Léon Fleuriot, Pierre-Yves Lambert and others in Études celtiques (1985); each proposed a different reading.

fuentes/tablilla-de-larzac/leer.0.titulo.texto: Michel Lejeune, “Two Gaulish magical inscriptions: the Chamalières lead; the Larzac lead” (1984), on Persée

fuentes/tablilla-de-larzac/leer.1.titulo.texto: Michel Lejeune, “Approaching the text”, in the Études celtiques edition (1985), on Persée

fuentes/tablilla-de-chamalieres/resumen.texto: Lead tablet measuring 6 by 4 centimeters, found in 1971 at the spring of the Roches at Chamalières (Puy-de-Dôme), a water sanctuary where thousands of wooden ex-votos representing bodies, heads and limbs came out. Its text, of 396 letters in 47 words, invokes Maponos Arvernatis, “Maponos the Arvernian”, “by the magic of those below” (brixtia anderon), and names several men. It is dated between 50 BC and AD 50.

fuentes/tablilla-de-chamalieres/por_que_.texto: It is the third longest Gaulish text, after the Larzac lead and the Coligny calendar, and one of the few witnesses to Maponos outside Britain. Because of its magical theme most read it as a curse (defixio), perhaps against opponents in a lawsuit; Wolfgang Meid, judging by the place and the ex-votos, read it as a prayer for healing. Its word-by-word translation remains disputed.

fuentes/tablilla-de-chamalieres/leer.0.t.texto: Michel Lejeune, “Two Gaulish magical inscriptions” (1984), on Persée

fuentes/inscripcion-de-penalba-de-villas.texto: Celtiberian and Latin, in Latin script; some in Iberian

Hundreds of inscriptions and carvings on a cliff one and a half kilometers long near Teruel, discovered by Juan Cabré in 1910 and dated almost all between the 1st century BC and the 1st century AD. Almost all are very short. The two longest are a passage of the Aeneid in Latin and a text in Celtiberian written in Latin letters that begins ENIOROSEI and names LVGVEI, which is read as the dative of Lugus: it is the only inscription that most accept as a mention of that god in the singular. There are also texts in Iberian script, and Cabré and local residents carried off several pieces, some now lost.

It is the main evidence for a Celtiberian sanctuary with names of gods, and the firmest support for the claim that Lugus was worshipped in the Iberian Peninsula. The reading of the main text remains disputed (Jürgen Untermann, Francisco Marco Simón, Dagmar Wodtko): it has been interpreted as a dedication, as a mention of a festival, or as a description of a rite.

fuentes/tablillas-de-bath/idioma_origina.texto: British Latin; perhaps some in Brittonic

fuentes/tablillas-de-bath/resumen.texto: Some 130 sheets found in 1979–1980 in the sacred spring of the temple of Sulis Minerva, at Bath, written between the 2nd and 4th centuries. Almost all ask the goddess to punish whoever stole something — a cloak, gloves, coins, a ring — until it is returned, and many of the petitioners' names are Celtic. Two are in a language that is not Latin, which has been proposed as Brittonic, without agreement among specialists. They were edited by Roger Tomlin in 1988.

fuentes/tablillas-de-bath/por_que_import.texto: They are the most direct voice of ordinary people who prayed to a British goddess with a Roman name, and they show how a local deity was integrated into Roman worship. They are on UNESCO's Memory of the World register for the United Kingdom.

fuentes/tablillas-de-bath/leer.0.titulo.texto: One of the tablets, with text and translation, in Roman Inscriptions of Britain

fuentes/inscripciones-a-lugus/titulo.texto: Inscriptions to Lugus and the Lugoves

fuentes/inscripciones-a-lugus/resumen.texto: Several dedications from the 1st century BC to the 3rd century AD, almost all from the Iberian Peninsula, to the Lugoves, in the plural. The best known is that of Uxama (Osma, Soria), where a certain Lucius Licinius dedicates an altar Lugovibus on behalf of the shoemakers' guild. At Avenches (Switzerland) the name LUGOVES appears on a capital, and there are others from the northwest of the peninsula, such as those from Lugo, with epithets that are sometimes feminine. In the singular, Lugus appears with certainty only at Peñalba de Villastar. In Gaul there are very few inscriptions, and the name survives in places such as Lugdunum (Lyon, Laon, Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges); in Britain and Ireland there are none.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-lugus/por_que_im.texto: They are the material basis for the reconstruction of a great god Lugus common to the Celts, proposed by Henri d'Arbois de Jubainville in 1884, linking him with Caesar's Gaulish Mercury and the Irish Lug. John Rhŷs added in 1888 the Welsh Lleu, who in the Mabinogi makes shoes with Gwydion. The reconstruction is disputed: there are no images of Lugus, the plural form suggests several gods (Henri Gaidoz already objected that a plural god could not be the principal one), and the etymology “light”, which made him a sun god, has phonetic difficulties pointed out, among others, by Garrett Olmsted.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-taranis/autor.texto: Devotees in Gaul, Germany, Britain and Dalmatia

fuentes/inscripciones-a-taranis/idioma_o.texto: Latin and Gaulish in Greek letters

fuentes/inscripciones-a-taranis/resumen.texto: A few scattered dedications to Taranis, Taranus, Tanarus or Taranucnus: one in Gaulish written in Greek letters from Orgon (Provence), in which a certain Vebrumaros offers something to Taranus; an altar from Chester to Jupiter Tanarus dated 154, dedicated by a man from Clunia, in Hispania; another to Jupiter Tanarus from Scardona (Dalmatia), and two to Taranucnus from Upper Germany. His name is linked to Welsh taran and Irish torann, “thunder”. In Gaul there are also images of a Jupiter with a wheel and a thunderbolt, such as the small statuette from Le Châtelet (Haute-Marne), which are attributed to him although no inscription confirms it.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-taranis/por_que_.texto: Taranis is the Celtic candidate for the Indo-European god of thunder (the Baltic Perkunas, the Germanic Thor, the Vedic Indra). Lucan is the only ancient author who names him, and from the few scattered inscriptions some deduce a minor cult and others a widespread one. That the god of the wheel is Taranis was argued by Lambrechts, Hatt and Anne Ross; Miranda Green rejects this and sees in the wheel a solar symbol, because no inscription links Taranis with the wheel.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-teutates/autor.texto: Devotees in Britain and on the frontiers of the Empire

fuentes/inscripciones-a-teutates/resumen.texto: A series of Latin dedications, almost all from the military frontiers of the Empire and above all from Britain, to Toutatis, Totatis or Teutates. When he is joined to a Roman god it is always Mars (Mars Toutatis, on a silver plaque from Barkway, Hertfordshire). In Gaul he is certain only on a stylus from Jort and on potsherds from Beauclair (Auvergne). There are also about 68 rings from the 2nd and 3rd centuries bearing the letters TOT, almost all from Lincolnshire, which Emil Hübner (1877) and later Anne Ross and Martin Henig read as an abbreviation of Totatis; Andreas Hofeneder and others prefer to read them as a formula of good wishes. His name comes from Proto-Celtic *toutā, “tribe, people”.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-teutates/por_que.texto: Because of the etymology he is interpreted as “god of the tribe”, and because of related names (Teutanus, Toutiorix) some hold that he was not a single god but a title that each people gave to its protector. Lucan names him together with Esus and Taranis, and the Bern scholia attribute to him victims drowned in a barrel; his modern fame owes much to Asterix (“By Toutatis!”).

fuentes/inscripciones-a-epona/autor.texto: Devotees in Gaul, on the Rhine, on the Danube and in Rome

fuentes/inscripciones-a-epona/resumen.texto: Epona, whose name derives from Celtic *epos, “horse”, is the Celtic goddess with the most evidence: the catalogue of Émile Thevenot, published with René Magnen's book (1953), already gathered 268 inscriptions and images, mainly from eastern Gaul and the Rhine and Danube frontiers, but also from Britain, the Balkans and Rome. The inscriptions are in Latin, rarely in Greek, and were dedicated above all by cavalrymen of the army, not only by Gauls. She is shown seated sideways on a mare or among horses and foals, with fruit or a patera. An Italian rural calendar (from Guidizzolo) fixes her festival on 18 December, and Juvenal (VIII.157), Apuleius (Metamorphoses III.27) and the Christian apologists Minucius Felix and Tertullian mention her images in stables.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-epona/por_que_im.texto: She had a cult in Rome itself, carried there by army cavalrymen, and it is often said that she is the only Gaulish deity to have had one, although there are also dedications to Belenus in Rome. She is compared with the Welsh Rhiannon and the Irish Macha, linked to horses and sovereignty; the comparison is suggestive, but there is no documentary link between them.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-belenos/autor.texto: Devotees of Aquileia, Noricum and Gaul

fuentes/inscripciones-a-belenos/resumen.texto: Some 51 dedications to Belenus, according to the count of Helmut Birkhan (2006), often as Apollo Belenus: most come from Aquileia (northern Italy), others from neighboring cities and from Noricum, and a few from southern Gaul (Marseille, Saint-Chamas, Saint-Rémy). Tertullian (Apology 24) names him as the god of the Norici; Herodian (VIII.3) tells that the defenders of Aquileia, besieged by the emperor Maximinus in 238, said they had seen him fighting for the city; Ausonius speaks of a guardian of his temple, a descendant of the druids.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-belenos/por_que_.texto: It shows how a god of Celtic origin became the patron of a Roman city and was assimilated to Apollo as a healer. His name was linked with the Irish festival of Beltaine and with a root meaning “bright”, which made him pass for a sun god; current linguistics debates both connections.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-las-matronas/aut.texto: Devotees of the lower Rhine and other provinces

fuentes/inscripciones-a-las-matronas/res.texto: More than 1,100 votive stones (Rudolf Simek's count), almost all from the 2nd and 3rd centuries and from the lower Rhine (around Cologne, Bonn and Jülich), dedicated to triads of seated mother goddesses, often wearing round headdresses, with local epithets such as Aufaniae or Vacallinehae. There are similar dedications to the Matres in Gaul, Britain, northern Italy and the Iberian Peninsula, among them one to the “Galician Mothers” (Matribus Gallaicis).

fuentes/inscripciones-a-las-matronas/por.texto: It is the best-documented cult of the Rhine frontier and a clear case of mixing: half of the epithets are Celtic and half Germanic, and the devotees were often soldiers and families of Romanized Ubii. Their relation to the Irish triple goddesses is a modern comparison.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-brigantia/resume.texto: Seven Latin dedications from the 2nd and 3rd centuries, from northern Britain, to Brigantia, the goddess of the Brigantes: two call her Victoria Brigantia (Greetland and Castleford), one Caelestis Brigantia (Corbridge), and another a nymph (Brampton). A relief from Birrens (southern Scotland), dedicated by the architect Amandus, shows her winged, with a mural crown and with the attributes of Minerva and Victory. No ancient author names her.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-brigantia/por_qu.texto: Her name, interpreted as “the high one” or “the exalted one”, is the same as that of the Irish Brigit, and hence the hypothesis of a great common goddess who passed into Saint Brigid; but as it is an epithet, it may have been applied to different goddesses. Martin Henig (1984) observed that all the datable dedications are from the time of Septimius Severus and Caracalla, and read her as a personification of the new province of Britannia Inferior rather than as an inherited goddess; Anne Ross, by contrast, made her a great Celtic goddess.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-brigantia/leer.0.texto: Birrens dedication to Brigantia (RIB 2091), in Roman Inscriptions of Britain

fuentes/inscripciones-a-sucellos/autor.texto: Devotees of Gaul and neighboring provinces

fuentes/inscripciones-a-sucellos/resumen.texto: About ten Latin inscriptions, according to Bernhard Maier, and many images of the “god with the mallet”: a mature, bearded man dressed in the Gaulish manner, with a long-handled mallet and a pot. They are concentrated in the valleys of the Rhône and Saône. On an altar from Sarrebourg, found in 1895, he appears with his consort, Nantosuelta, with both their names, and Jan de Vries counted thirteen monuments on which they appear together. No ancient author names him.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-sucellos/por_que.texto: His name is interpreted as “the good striker”. He has been read as a god of abundance and wine, or as a god of the underworld, and compared with the Roman Silvanus and with the Irish Dagda, with his club and his cauldron; his character remains disputed.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-maponos/resumen.texto: Six Latin dedications from military sites in northern Britain, near Hadrian's Wall — three from Corbridge, others from Ribchester, Brampton and Vindolanda — four of them to Apollo Maponos, often by army officers; his name in Gaulish on the Chamalières tablet, and the place name Locus Maponi (today Lochmaben, in southern Scotland), given by the Ravenna Cosmography. His name means “divine son”. No image can be attributed to him with certainty.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-maponos/por_que_.texto: He is considered a forerunner of Mabon, son of Modron (from *Matrona, “the mother”), the prisoner whom Arthur's men free in the Welsh tale of Culhwch and Olwen, and he is compared with the Irish Mac ind Óc. No ancient author names him.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-nodens/escrita.l.texto: Temple of Nodens at Lydney Park

fuentes/inscripciones-a-nodens/resumen.texto: The dedications from the sanctuary at Lydney Park (Gloucestershire), among them a lead sheet in which Silvianus, who lost a ring, offers Nodens half its value and asks him to deny health to a certain Senicianus until he returns it to the temple; and two statuettes from Cockersand Moss (Lancashire) dedicated to Mars Nodens.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-nodens/por_que_i.texto: The name was linked with the Irish Nuadu and the Welsh Nudd or Lludd. J. R. R. Tolkien wrote a note on its etymology in 1932 for the excavation report, and a gold ring bearing the name of Senicianus, found in the 18th century, was later connected, without direct proof, with the ring mentioned in the curse.

fuentes/inscripciones-a-nodens/leer.0.ti.texto: Silvianus's curse against Senicianus (RIB 306), in Roman Inscriptions of Britain

fuentes/inscripciones-a-dioses-del-oeste.texto: Inscriptions to the gods of western Hispania

Hundreds of Latin altars from the western peninsula, from Lusitania and Gallaecia, dedicated to native gods: Bandua, Navia, Reue, Cosus, Trebaruna, Ataecina, Endovellicus. Many carry local epithets, sometimes masculine and sometimes feminine, and they are almost never identified with Roman gods. Endovellicus had a sanctuary with dozens of altars at São Miguel da Mota (Alentejo) until the 5th century.

They show the richest native religion of the peninsula, with gods who do not appear in Gaul or Britain. Whether they are “Celtic” is disputed: several linguists, such as Jürgen Untermann and Blanca María Prósper, connect the names with Lusitanian, an Indo-European language that many do not consider Celtic.

fuentes/escolios-de-berna-a-lucano/resum.texto: Explanatory notes to Lucan's poem, copied in a 9th-century manuscript from Bern, with layers that may go back to the 4th century. On the passage about the three Gaulish gods (Pharsalia I.444–446), they say that Teutates was sacrificed by a man being put head first into a barrel until he drowned, Esus by being hanged from a tree until he bled to death, and Taranis by burning several people in a wooden vessel. They also give two Roman equivalents for each: Teutates with Mercury or Mars, Esus with Mars or Mercury, Taranis with Dis Pater or Jupiter.

fuentes/escolios-de-berna-a-lucano/por_q.texto: It is the only source that assigns a form of death to each god, and from it comes the theory of the “triple death” applied to the Lindow Man. Since it is late, anonymous and self-contradictory, many (Hutton, Maier) consider it a learned elaboration based on Caesar and Lucan rather than an independent witness.

fuentes/sermones-de-cesareo-de-arles/res.texto: About 250 sermons written by the bishop of Arles to be read in the parishes of southern Gaul. Several condemn Christians who make vows or eat beside trees, springs and stones, consult diviners and enchanters, and who on the January calends cover themselves with skins and animal heads and disguise themselves “as a deer or a vetula” (an old woman or a heifer, depending on how the word is read).

fuentes/sermones-de-cesareo-de-arles/por.texto: Together with the canons of church councils, it shows that a century after the prohibition of pagan worship, rites persisted in the Gaulish countryside. Whether they were remnants of Celtic religion, of Roman religion, or customs with no belief behind them is debated, and many passages were later copied in other regions as formulas.

fuentes/canones-de-los-concilios-galos/t.texto: Canons of the Gaulish councils against pagan cults

fuentes/canones-de-los-concilios-galos/r.texto: Provisions of several Gaulish councils against open-air cults: the so-called second Council of Arles (5th century) orders that whoever lights torches or venerates trees, springs or stones be rebuked; the Council of Tours of 567 asks that whoever practices pagan rites before stones, trees or springs be cut off from the Church; the synod of Auxerre, from the late 6th century, prohibits fulfilling vows among brambles, sacred trees or springs.

fuentes/canones-de-los-concilios-galos/p.texto: They show that the open-air cults described by the ancient authors were still alive, or at least a concern, in Merovingian Gaul. That they are repeated almost word for word from one council to another suggests that they were sometimes inherited formulas rather than descriptions of what was actually happening.

fuentes/de-correctione-rusticorum/resume.texto: A model sermon that Martin of Braga wrote around 572 for Bishop Polemius of Astorga to preach to the peasants of Gallaecia. It explains that the demons cast out of heaven made themselves worshipped as gods — Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, Venus, Neptune in the sea, the lamiae in the rivers, the nymphs in the springs, Diana in the woods — and it condemns lighting candles beside stones, trees, springs and crossroads, throwing bread into springs, observing the days of the gods, and celebrating the January calends.

fuentes/de-correctione-rusticorum/por_qu.texto: It is the most detailed text on the rural cults of northwestern Iberia in the 6th century, and Galician Celticism read it as proof of a living Celtic religion. But the names it uses are Roman, and much of the sermon follows Caesarius of Arles and the tradition of the Church Fathers; scholars debate what it really describes of Gallaecia and what is formula.

fuentes/codigo-teodosiano/autor.texto: Commission of jurists of Theodosius II

fuentes/codigo-teodosiano/resumen.texto: The official compilation of the laws of the Christian emperors since Constantine, published by Theodosius II in 438. Title 10 of Book XVI gathers the laws against paganism, among them those of Theodosius I of 391 and 392 that banned sacrifices, access to temples and all pagan worship, even domestic worship.

fuentes/codigo-teodosiano/por_que_import.texto: It marks the legal end of pagan cults in the Empire, including those of the Gallo-Roman and British peoples. Archaeology shows that many rural sanctuaries remained in use for some decades more, and that their abandonment was gradual and uneven.

fuentes/gloria-de-los-confesores/titulo.texto: Book of the Glory of the Confessors

fuentes/gloria-de-los-confesores/resumen.texto: A collection of miracles of Gaulish saints written by Gregory of Tours. In chapter 2 he recounts that on Mount Helanus, in the Gévaudan, there was a lake to which the peasants brought offerings each year — clothing, linen, cheese, wax, bread — and threw them into the water during three days of feasting, until a bishop built a church there to Saint Hilary and persuaded them to bring their offerings to it instead. In another chapter he tells that at Autun the image of Berecynthia, a mother goddess, was paraded on a cart through the fields in the time of Bishop Simplicius.

fuentes/gloria-de-los-confesores/por_que.texto: The lake is identified with that of Saint-Andéol, in the Aubrac, where pilgrimages continued until the 19th century: it is one of the clearest cases of the continuity of offerings in water and of their Christianization. Berecynthia is a name of the Roman Cybele, and it is not known whether it concealed a local goddess.

fuentes/lebor-gabala-erenn/titulo.texto: Book of the Invasions of Ireland (Lebor Gabála Érenn)

fuentes/lebor-gabala-erenn/resumen.texto: A compilation from the 11th century, in prose and verse, that tells the history of Ireland from Creation as a series of six occupations: the people of Cessair, that of Partholón, that of Nemed, the Fir Bolg, the Tuatha Dé Danann, and the sons of Míl, ancestors of the Gaels, who arrive from Hispania. The Tuatha Dé Danann, who in other texts are gods, appear here as a defeated people of magicians who withdraw beneath the burial mounds (síde). Everything is fitted into biblical chronology and Noah's genealogy.

fuentes/lebor-gabala-erenn/por_que_impor.texto: It was accepted as history until the 17th century, and it is the main source on the Irish gods, turned into human ancestors. For John Carey and Kim McCone it is a “synthetic pseudohistory” by Christian scholars who imitated Isidore and Orosius; nativists see in its names and episodes remnants of older myths. The journey of the sons of Míl from Hispania fed Galician Celticism in the 19th century.

fuentes/cath-maige-tuired/titulo.texto: The Second Battle of Mag Tuired (Cath Maige Tuired)

fuentes/cath-maige-tuired/resumen.texto: An account from the mythological cycle preserved in a single 16th-century manuscript, whose language points to the 9th century, with later additions. It tells how the Tuatha Dé Danann, led by King Nuadu, who lost a hand and got it back in silver, and by Lug, who masters all the arts, defeat the Fomorians at Mag Tuired; the Dagda with his cauldron and his club, the Morrígan, Ogma, the smith Goibniu and the physician Dian Cécht take part.

fuentes/cath-maige-tuired/por_que_import.texto: It is the main text on the Irish gods in action. Dumézil and his followers read it as an Indo-European myth of war between two classes of gods (comparable to the war between the Æsir and the Vanir in Scandinavia), and Lug is linked with Caesar's Gaulish Mercury, “inventor of all the arts”. Anti-nativists stress that it is a composition by Christian scholars, with echoes of the story of Troy and of the Bible.

fuentes/cath-maige-tuired/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by Elizabeth Gray (CELT, University College Cork)

fuentes/cath-maige-tuired/leer.1.titulo.texto: Irish text edited by Elizabeth Gray (CELT)

fuentes/dindshenchas/resumen.texto: A collection of about 176 poems and prose tales that explain the origin of the names of places in Ireland — hills, rivers, lakes, fortresses — with episodes of gods, heroes and kings. The first recension survives in the Book of Leinster (around 1160), the second in manuscripts of the 14th and 15th centuries, and the poems were edited by Edward Gwynn (1903–1935). It explains, for example, the name of the River Boyne through the goddess Bóand, and tells that at Mag Slécht an idol of gold, Crom Crúaich, surrounded by twelve of stone, was worshipped, and children were sacrificed to it until Patrick arrived.

fuentes/dindshenchas/por_que_importa.texto: It is the great repertory of Irish sacred geography and one of the few texts that describe a pagan cult with sacrifices in Ireland. But its tales are learned etymologies, sometimes invented to explain a name, and how much they preserve of ancient beliefs is debated.

fuentes/dindshenchas/leer.0.titulo.texto: The metrical Dindshenchas, edition and translation by Edward Gwynn, first part (CELT)

fuentes/sanas-cormaic/resumen.texto: A glossary of more than 1,400 difficult or archaic Irish words, with explanations and etymologies, attributed in its oldest version to Cormac mac Cuilennáin, king and bishop of Munster. Among its entries are Brigit, “a poetess, daughter of the Dagda”, venerated by poets, with two sisters of the same name, one a physician and the other a smith; Beltaine, explained as “lucky fire”: two fires that the druids kindled with charms to drive livestock between them against disease; and Imbolc (oímelc), as the time of ewes' milk.

fuentes/sanas-cormaic/por_que_importa.texto: It is the written basis of almost everything asserted about Brigit as a goddess and about the rites of Beltaine. But its etymologies are often fanciful, and they were written four centuries after Christianization, so its value as evidence of pagan religion is debated (Hutton).

fuentes/tochmarc-emire/resumen.texto: A tale of the Ulster cycle about how Cú Chulainn courts Emer and trains in arms with the warrior woman Scáthach. In the riddle dialogue between the two, the four festivals that divide the year are named: Samain, Imbolc, Beltaine and Brón Trogain, the beginning of the harvest, an old name for Lughnasadh.

fuentes/tochmarc-emire/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the oldest texts that list together the four festivals of the Irish calendar, the basis of everything asserted about the “Celtic year”. That they existed as festivals does not mean they had the religious meaning that the 19th century attributed to them.

fuentes/coraza-de-patricio/resumen.texto: A prayer of protection that tradition attributes to Patrick, although its language is from the 8th century. The one who recites it invokes the Trinity and the forces of creation — the sun, fire, lightning, wind, sea, earth, rock — and asks for defense “against the spells of women, of smiths and of druids”.

fuentes/coraza-de-patricio/por_que_impor.texto: It shows that in Christian Ireland of the 8th century the druid was still a feared figure as a sorcerer, and that Christian prayer adopted the form of protective charms. The invocation of the elements has been read as pagan inheritance, although it has parallels in the liturgy and in Latin loricae.

fuentes/coraza-de-patricio/leer.0.titulo.texto: Irish text and English translation by Stokes and Strachan on Wikisource

fuentes/la-rama-dorada/resumen.texto: A comparative study of magic and religion that starts from the priest-king of the grove of Nemi and gathers customs from around the world as remnants of fertility cults and of the sacrificed sacred king. It interprets the bonfires of Beltaine and of Halloween, with their games of chance, as remnants of Celtic human sacrifices, and Samhain as a festival of the dead and the new year.

fuentes/la-rama-dorada/por_que_importa.texto: It spread many of the ideas about Celtic festivals that still circulate, including that of Halloween as a Druidic inheritance. Anthropology abandoned its method, which joined data from different periods and places without context, and Hutton showed that its interpretations of British festivals have no documentary support.

fuentes/celtic-heathendom-rhys/titulo.texto: Lectures on the Origin and Growth of Religion as Illustrated by Celtic Heathendom

fuentes/celtic-heathendom-rhys/resumen.texto: The Hibbert Lectures that Rhŷs gave in 1886: they reconstruct a Celtic pantheon from Welsh and Irish mythology, with solar and sky gods according to Max Müller's comparative mythology, and present 1 November as the beginning of the Celtic year.

fuentes/celtic-heathendom-rhys/por_que_i.texto: They were the first academic synthesis of Celtic religion in English, and the origin of the idea of Samain as the new year, which passed to Frazer and from there to popular culture. The solar interpretation of the gods was abandoned, and Hutton showed that the November New Year rested on modern Welsh and Manx customs.

fuentes/ideologia-tripartita-dumezil/tit.texto: The Tripartite Ideology of the Indo-Europeans

fuentes/ideologia-tripartita-dumezil/res.texto: A synthesis of the theory that Dumézil had been developing since 1938: the Indo-European peoples organized their thought into three hierarchical functions — magical and legal sovereignty, warrior force, fertility and abundance — visible in the castes of India, in the Roman triad of Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus, and in Gaul in the druids, the knights and the common people that Caesar describes.

fuentes/ideologia-tripartita-dumezil/por.texto: It gave Celtic studies their most influential comparative framework, followed by Sjoestedt, de Vries, Le Roux and Guyonvarc'h. Critics (Wouter Belier, 1991; Bruce Lincoln; Colin Renfrew) argue that the scheme is so elastic that it can be found in any society, and that Caesar's division reflects the Roman point of view rather than a Gaulish ideology.

fuentes/decayed-gods-belier/titulo.texto: Decayed Gods: Origin and Development of Georges Dumézil's «Idéologie tripartite»

fuentes/decayed-gods-belier/resumen.texto: A critical review of Dumézil's entire work. It argues that the theory of the three functions was built by choosing the data that confirm it and discarding the rest, and that it changed its formulation so many times that it cannot be refuted.

fuentes/decayed-gods-belier/por_que_impo.texto: It is the most systematic critique of Dumézil, and the one usually cited by those who distrust Indo-European comparison applied to the Celts. Critics of this review reply that comparison of vocabulary, names and formulas remains valid even if the tripartite scheme is not.

fuentes/dioses-y-heroes-de-los-celtas/ti.texto: Gods and Heroes of the Celts

fuentes/dioses-y-heroes-de-los-celtas/re.texto: A brief essay that reads Irish mythology and the Gaulish evidence as a religious system: tribal gods, such as the Gaulish Teutates, set against earth and sovereignty goddesses tied to places, with the warrior hero as the central figure. Myles Dillon translated it into English in 1949.

fuentes/dioses-y-heroes-de-los-celtas/po.texto: It was the first modern synthesis of Celtic religion using a comparative method, and one of the foundations of the nativist reading. It has been objected that it treats medieval Irish texts and ancient Gaulish testimonies as if they were one and the same religion.

fuentes/keltische-religion/resumen.texto: A handbook that orders the Gaulish, British and Irish evidence according to Dumézil's theory and seeks equivalents with Germanic religion: the Irish Lug and the Gaulish Mercury with Odin, Taranis with Thor, and the three functions in the gods of Caesar.

fuentes/keltische-religion/por_que_impor.texto: For decades it was the reference synthesis on the Continent. It is criticized for its trust in comparison and in late Irish texts, and his work on Germanic subjects has been reassessed because of his collaboration with Nazism.

fuentes/comparative-mythology-puhvel/res.texto: A handbook of comparative Indo-European mythology, with chapters on India, Iran, Greece, Rome, the Germanic peoples and the Celts. It relates the rite of the mare of Tír Conaill recounted by Gerald of Wales to the Vedic horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) and the Roman October Horse, as remnants of an Indo-European rite of sovereignty.

fuentes/comparative-mythology-puhvel/por.texto: It is the most cited text on the Indo-European heritage of the horse and sovereignty. The comparison depends on a single hostile medieval witness, that of Gerald of Wales, and on structural similarities that other authors consider forced.

fuentes/indo-european-poetry-and-myth/re.texto: A compendium of what the comparison of languages, poetic formulas and myths allows us to reconstruct of Indo-European religion and poetry: the sky father, the thunder god, the sun and dawn, the divine twins, the poet as sage. It uses Celtic data to show, among other things, the common word for “god” (Gaulish dēuos, Irish día), the figure of the poet and the seer, and formulas of imperishable fame.

fuentes/indo-european-poetry-and-myth/po.texto: It is the current reference for Indo-European comparison, and it carefully separates what rests on cognate words from mere thematic resemblance. It acknowledges that in the Celtic case the correspondences are weaker than in India, Greece or the Germanic world, because the texts are late and Christian.

fuentes/celtic-mythology-mac-cana/resume.texto: An illustrated synthesis that brings together the Gaulish and British gods of the inscriptions and those of the Irish and Welsh texts, and argues that medieval literature preserves, under Christian editing, a pre-Christian mythological tradition: the goddess of sovereignty, the otherworld, the festivals, sacred kingship.

fuentes/celtic-mythology-mac-cana/por_qu.texto: It is the clearest statement of the nativist position. McCone and Carey object that the same features can be explained as the creation of Christian scholars who knew the Bible and the classics.

fuentes/pagan-celtic-britain/titulo.texto: Pagan Celtic Britain: Studies in Iconography and Tradition

fuentes/pagan-celtic-britain/resumen.texto: A catalogue and interpretation of the religious images and inscriptions of prehistoric and Roman Britain, arranged by theme: the head, horned gods, goddesses, sacred animals. It argues that the human head was the central religious symbol of the Celts, and reads the images with the help of the Irish texts.

fuentes/pagan-celtic-britain/por_que_imp.texto: For decades it was the reference on British religious iconography, and it established the idea of a “cult of the head”. Later criticism (Hutton, Simon James) points out that it groups objects from very different periods and places, and explains them with Irish texts a thousand years later.

fuentes/the-gods-of-the-celts/resumen.texto: An archaeological synthesis of the cults of Roman Gaul and Britain: gods of the sun and sky, of war, of fertility, of waters and of animals, arranged according to their images and inscriptions.

fuentes/the-gods-of-the-celts/por_que_im.texto: It is the most used handbook on the Gallo-Roman and British gods. It has been criticized for grouping by theme images from different contexts, and for presenting as “Celtic” cults that are largely creations of the Roman period.

fuentes/die-religion-der-kelten/resumen.texto: A synthesis that goes through the sources in order — archaeology, Greek and Roman authors, inscriptions, medieval texts — and on each theme separates what each type of source says before comparing them. It distrusts reconstructing a single pan-Celtic religion.

fuentes/die-religion-der-kelten/por_que_.texto: It is one of the most cautious syntheses, and the one that best distinguishes evidence from interpretation. Because of its caution, it leaves open many questions that other authors close through comparison.

fuentes/gods-of-the-celts-and-the-indo-e.texto: The Gods of the Celts and the Indo-Europeans

An attempt to reconstruct the complete Celtic pantheon and relate it to the Indo-European one, pairing Gaulish, Irish and Welsh gods and reading the Gundestrup cauldron and the Coligny calendar within that system.
It is the most ambitious attempt at systematization. Most reviewers consider it too speculative: many equivalences rest only on similarities of function or image.

fuentes/dioses-de-la-hispania-celtica/re.texto: A study of the inscriptions to native gods of the peninsula. It orders them by region and by their spread, and shows that Bandua, Navia, Reue or Cosus are concentrated in the west, that the cult of Lugus is limited to a few places, and that in Celtiberia there are very few theonyms.

fuentes/dioses-de-la-hispania-celtica/po.texto: It is the current basis for speaking about the pre-Roman gods of Hispania with evidence. It leaves open, as almost all do, whether the gods of the west are Celtic or Lusitanian.

fuentes/the-druids-kendrick/titulo.texto: The Druids: A Study in Keltic Prehistory

fuentes/the-druids-kendrick/resumen.texto: It gathers and translates all the ancient texts on the druids and compares them with the archaeology of its time, separating them from the theories of antiquarians who, since the 17th century, linked them with the megaliths.

fuentes/the-druids-kendrick/por_que_impo.texto: It was the first academic study of the subject, and it separated the ancient druids from modern Druidism. Its view of the druids as priests of a primitive religion and its ideas about the Iron Age have been superseded.

fuentes/the-druids-piggott/titulo.texto: The Druids: A Study in Keltic Prehistory

fuentes/the-druids-piggott/resumen.texto: It separates three druids: the one of the ancient texts, the one of archaeology, and the one invented by antiquarians and Romantics from the Renaissance onward. Among the ancient authors it distinguishes a “Posidonian” tradition, often unfavorable and centered on sacrifices, and an “Alexandrian” one, of idealized primitivism, which makes them the sages of a golden age (Diogenes Laertius, Clement). It treats the druids as a phenomenon of the Iron Age, unrelated to the megaliths.

fuentes/the-druids-piggott/por_que_impor.texto: It fixed modern criticism of the Romantic druid and the distinction between sources. It has been criticized for being itself disparaging toward the Celts, and for relying on an archaeology of “invasion” that is now abandoned.

fuentes/les-druides-le-roux/titulo.texto: The Druids: A Study in Keltic Prehistory

fuentes/les-druides-le-roux/resumen.texto: Written with Christian-J. Guyonvarc'h on the basis of Le Roux's 1961 work: it reconstructs Druidism as a priesthood common to all Celts, with its theology, its calendar and its teaching, drawing above all on Irish texts and Dumézil's theory.

fuentes/les-druides-le-roux/por_que_impo.texto: It had wide circulation in France and in modern Druidism. Historians and archaeologists criticize it for projecting onto ancient Gaul institutions described a thousand years later in Ireland, and for treating tradition as timeless.

fuentes/webster-at-the-end-of-the-world/.texto: At the End of the World: Druidic and Other Revitalization Movements in Post-Conquest Gaul and Britain

An article in the journal Britannia arguing that the Roman prohibition of Druidism was political: after the conquest, druids led movements of resistance and prophecy, such as that of Maricus and the druidic prophecy of 69–70, comparable to the millenarian movements of other colonized peoples.

It changed the reading of the prohibition, which can no longer be explained only by the Roman rejection of human sacrifice. It has been objected that the texts about rebellious druids are few, and that the colonial comparison assumes more organization than can be proved.

fuentes/webster-creolizing/resumen.texto: An article in the American Journal of Archaeology proposing that Gallo-Roman and Romano-British gods, with their double names (Sulis Minerva, Mars Lenus), be read not as a peaceful fusion but as “creolization”: provincials adopted Roman forms and gave them their own meanings, sometimes of resistance.

fuentes/webster-creolizing/por_que_impor.texto: It is the most cited critique of the model of interpretatio romana as simple translation. Other archaeologists reply that the word “creolization” carries into antiquity a model drawn from American slave societies.

fuentes/les-religions-gauloises/resumen.texto: Synthesis of what the excavation of sanctuaries in northern Gaul (Gournay, Ribemont) reveals about the rites of independent Gaul: enclosures with ditches, display of weapons and trophies, animal sacrifices with the meat shared out, and a cult of the gods without images until the Roman period.

fuentes/les-religions-gauloises/por_que_.texto: It put the archaeology of sanctuaries at the centre of the study of Gaulish religion. His interpretations of human bones as warrior trophies, and his reliance on Posidonius to read them, are debated.

fuentes/les-druides-brunaux/titulo.texto: The Druids: Philosophers among the Barbarians

fuentes/les-druides-brunaux/resumen.texto: Argues that the druids were an elite of sages comparable to Greek philosophers, influenced by Pythagoreanism through Massalia, and that Posidonius, who met them on his journey, is a reliable source; he reconstructs their doctrine, their political role and their decline in the 1st century BC.

fuentes/les-druides-brunaux/por_que_impo.texto: It rehabilitates the image of the druids with archaeological support. Its critics (among them Hutton) hold that the image of Pythagorean philosophers is a Greek construction and that Brunaux takes for reality what is the interpretation of ancient authors.

fuentes/caesars-druids/titulo.texto: Caesar's Druids: Story of an Ancient Priesthood

fuentes/caesars-druids/resumen.texto: Reviews the ancient texts and the archaeology that can be related to the druids—burials with medical or divinatory instruments, such as that of the “doctor” of Stanway, and bodies from the bogs—and presents them as a real priesthood with functions of divination, medicine and sacrifice.

fuentes/caesars-druids/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most recent synthesis that relies on linking specific objects to the druids. No archaeological find can be attributed with certainty to a druid, and critics such as Hutton consider these attributions speculative.

fuentes/dying-for-the-gods/titulo.texto: Dying for the Gods: Human Sacrifice in Iron Age and Roman Europe

fuentes/dying-for-the-gods/resumen.texto: Gathers the ancient texts on human sacrifice among the Gauls, Britons and Germans, and the archaeological cases that can be related to it: the bodies from the bogs, the human bones of Gournay and Ribemont, the dead of Acy-Romance, the skulls of Entremont and Roquepertuse. It argues that human sacrifice existed as a religious practice in circumstances of crisis, although it was rarer than Roman authors say.

fuentes/dying-for-the-gods/por_que_impor.texto: It is the most complete study in favour of the reality of Celtic human sacrifice. Critics (Hutton, Briggs) object that many violent deaths may be executions, murders or treatments of corpses without sacrifice, and that the religious reading depends on the same Roman texts that it sets out to verify.

fuentes/blood-and-mistletoe/titulo.texto: Blood and Mistletoe: The History of the Druids in Britain

fuentes/blood-and-mistletoe/resumen.texto: History of the images of the druids from the ancient authors to neo-druidism, with the thesis that almost everything that is “known” about them is reconstruction: each era imagined them as it needed (patriots, philosophers, bloodthirsty priests, ecologists), and the ancient sources, scarce and second-hand, do not allow going much further.

fuentes/blood-and-mistletoe/por_que_impo.texto: It is the most complete critique of the romantic druid and of the nationalist and religious use of the druids. It has been objected that its scepticism sets aside what comparison and archaeology allow us to infer.

fuentes/pagan-religions-hutton/titulo.texto: The Pagan Religions of the Ancient British Isles: Their Nature and Legacy

fuentes/pagan-religions-hutton/resumen.texto: Surveys the religion of Britain and Ireland from the Palaeolithic to Christianization and argues that almost everything is uncertain: archaeology shows rites but not beliefs, the classical texts come from outsiders, and the Irish and Welsh are Christians. He denies that the continuity of most supposed pagan survivals can be proven.

fuentes/pagan-religions-hutton/por_que_i.texto: It changed the tone of the discussion in the English-speaking world and spread the scepticism that folklorists had been raising since the 1970s about supposed pagan survivals. Celticists such as Mac Cana and archaeologists such as Aldhouse-Green accept more continuity than he does; criticism from feminism and neopaganism (such as that of Max Dashu) reproached him for his scepticism, and Hutton himself revised his approach in Pagan Britain (2013).

fuentes/the-stations-of-the-sun/titulo.texto: The Stations of the Sun: A History of the Ritual Year in Britain

fuentes/the-stations-of-the-sun/resumen.texto: Documented history of each festival of the British and Irish year. It argues that Samain is an Irish festival of the beginning of winter, with no evidence that it was a New Year or a festival of the dead before the Middle Ages; that All Saints was set on 1 November on the initiative of Rome and the Germanic world, not the Irish; and that Halloween results from the fusion of the two traditions.

fuentes/the-stations-of-the-sun/por_que_.texto: It is the main critique of the idea of Halloween as a druidic festival. Hutton does not deny that there was a great pagan festival in early November, but he denies that we know what rites it had. Other authors (among them Mac Cana) accept more continuity between Samain and medieval beliefs about the otherworld, and the date of All Saints is disputed with him, because the churches of Ireland and Northumbria, closely linked to each other, already celebrated it on 1 November around 800.

fuentes/carey-irish-national-origin-lege.texto: The Irish National Origin-Legend: Synthetic Pseudohistory

Lecture analysing how Irish scholars of the 7th to 11th centuries built the account of the invasions of Ireland by combining the Bible, Isidore, Orosius and local traditions, until they reached the Lebor Gabála Érenn.
It is the standard reading of the Lebor Gabála as a work of Christian scholarship. Nativists accept that elaboration, but maintain that the gods and episodes it arranges are older.

fuentes/the-passage-of-arms/titulo.texto: The Passage of Arms: An Archaeological Analysis of Prehistoric Hoards and Votive Deposits

fuentes/the-passage-of-arms/resumen.texto: Studies deposits of metal objects in rivers, lakes and bogs of north-western Europe and argues that they were deliberate offerings, not hoards or losses, in a practice that begins in the Neolithic, grows in the Bronze Age and continues in the Iron Age.

fuentes/the-passage-of-arms/por_que_impo.texto: It is the basis of the idea of a ritual continuity prior to the Celts and not tied to them. In each case it is debated whether a deposit is an offering, and whether continuity of the practice implies continuity of beliefs.

fuentes/lindow-man-body-in-the-bog/titul.texto: Lindow Man: The Body in the Bog

fuentes/lindow-man-body-in-the-bog/autor.texto: Ian Stead, John Bourke and Don Brothwell (eds.)

fuentes/lindow-man-body-in-the-bog/resum.texto: The British Museum's first scientific report on the Lindow Man: it describes a blow to the head, a cord around the neck and a cut in the throat, the contents of the stomach and the first radiocarbon dates, and proposes that it was a ritual death.

fuentes/lindow-man-body-in-the-bog/por_q.texto: It fixed the image of the “sacrificed Lindow Man”. Later reviews (Briggs, 1995; Joy, 2009) questioned the date and whether all the wounds were inflicted during life.

fuentes/life-and-death-of-a-druid-prince.texto: The Life and Death of a Druid Prince

Written with the chemist Don Robins: it argues that the Lindow Man was a druid prince who sacrificed himself voluntarily at Beltaine, around the year 60, to ask the gods to halt the Roman conquest, with a triple death for three gods, according to the Bern scholia.

It had wide popular circulation and is the classic example of an interpretation that goes beyond the evidence: neither the date, nor the rank, nor the season, nor the druidic character can be proven, and almost all specialists reject it.

fuentes/did-they-fall-or-were-they-pushe.texto: Did They Fall or Were They Pushed? Some Unresolved Questions about Bog Bodies

Chapter in the volume Bog Bodies: New Discoveries and New Perspectives (British Museum, 1995) that reviews the thesis of ritual sacrifice: it points out that many wounds may have been produced after death, by the weight of the peat or during extraction, and that among the bog bodies there are executed, murdered and accidental deaths, so that wounds to the neck or head are not enough to speak of sacrifice.

It is the reference critique of the use of bog bodies as proof of Celtic human sacrifice. Defenders of the ritual reading reply that the accumulation of wounds in some cases cannot be explained by accidents.

fuentes/kingship-and-sacrifice-kelly/tit.texto: Kingship and Sacrifice: Iron Age Bog Bodies and Boundaries

fuentes/kingship-and-sacrifice-kelly/res.texto: Guide by Eamonn Kelly, curator at the National Museum of Ireland, who argues that the Old Croghan and Clonycavan men, and other Irish bodies, were failed kings or rivals sacrificed at the boundaries of kingdoms, in relation to the ritual marriage between the king and the earth goddess of the Irish texts.

fuentes/kingship-and-sacrifice-kelly/por.texto: It is the most widespread interpretation of the Irish bodies. It joins Iron Age finds with medieval texts on kingship, which is why sceptics consider it an attractive but unproven hypothesis.

fuentes/origen-del-caldero-de-gundestrup.texto: The Origin of the Gundestrup Cauldron
A. K. Bergquist and T. F. Taylor

Article in the journal Antiquity that, on the basis of the silverwork technique, the style and the motifs (elephants, figures of Indian type), argues that the cauldron was made by Thracian goldsmiths of the lower Danube, perhaps for Celtic clients such as the Scordisci, and that it reached Denmark as booty or a gift.

It displaced the idea of a Gaulish cauldron made for druidic rites. Flemming Kaul and others went further and read the scenes in a Thracian key too (Thracian Tales on the Gundestrup Cauldron, 1991); Garrett Olmsted, by contrast, attributes the cauldron to workshops in north-western Gaul and sees in it Celtic gods and stories. The Thracian thesis is today the most accepted one regarding the technique and the workshop, not the meaning.

fuentes/llyn-cerrig-bach-fox/titulo.texto: A Find of the Early Iron Age from Llyn Cerrig Bach, Anglesey

fuentes/llyn-cerrig-bach-fox/resumen.texto: National Museum of Wales publication on the objects found in 1942: weapons, chariot and harness fittings, cauldrons, a trumpet and two slave chains. Fox argued that they were offerings thrown into the lake from a rock and came from much of Britain and Ireland, and linked them to the druidic sanctuary of Mona destroyed by Suetonius Paulinus.

fuentes/llyn-cerrig-bach-fox/por_que_imp.texto: It fixed the votive reading of the deposit, which is accepted today. The link with Tacitus's druids is a hypothesis: the dates of the objects are spread over several centuries.

fuentes/informe-de-lydney-park/titulo.texto: Report on the Excavation of the Prehistoric, Roman and Post-Roman Site in Lydney Park, Gloucestershire

fuentes/informe-de-lydney-park/resumen.texto: Report of the excavations of 1928-1929 at the temple of Nodens, with the temple, the guest house, the baths, the portico interpreted as a dormitory for healing by sleep, the offerings and the inscriptions. It includes an appendix by J. R. R. Tolkien, then professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford, on the etymology of the name Nodens.

fuentes/informe-de-lydney-park/por_que_i.texto: It is the basis of what is known about the sanctuary. Its dating of the temple to after 364 was later disputed, and many place it earlier, in the 3rd century; Tolkien's appendix is cited for its relation to the mythology he himself invented.

fuentes/etica-y-ritual-sopena/titulo.texto: Ethics and Ritual: An Approach to the Study of the Religiosity of the Celtiberian Peoples

fuentes/etica-y-ritual-sopena/resumen.texto: Study of the religion of the Celtiberians based on Greek and Latin texts, the iconography of pottery and stelae, and funerary archaeology: the warrior ethic, the exposure of those who died in combat to vultures, the devotio and rites of passage.

fuentes/etica-y-ritual-sopena/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the reference syntheses on Celtiberian religion. Like almost all research on the subject, it depends on few texts, written by the conquerors, and on images whose religious reading is interpretation.

personas/martin-de-tours/resumen.texto: Son of a Roman officer from Pannonia, he left the army, founded the monastery of Ligugé and was bishop of Tours from 371. His disciple Sulpicius Severus recounts in the Life of Saint Martin and in the Dialogues that he toured the Gaulish countryside knocking down temples and sacred trees and raising churches in their place. It is hagiography written during the saint's lifetime to make him a model bishop, and it exaggerates the miracles, but it is the most direct testimony of how the rural cults of Gaul came to an end; Martin became the most venerated saint of Merovingian Gaul.

personas/cesareo-de-arles/resumen.texto: Bishop of Arles from 502 to 542. His sermons to the people condemn vows and banquets beside trees, springs and stones, and the animal disguises of the Kalends of January, and they are one of the main sources on the practices that survived in Christian Gaul.

personas/martin-de-braga/resumen.texto: Monk born in Pannonia who arrived in Gallaecia around 550, brought the Suevi from Arianism to Catholicism, and became bishop and later metropolitan of Braga. His sermon De correctione rusticorum, from around 572, lists the rural cults of the north-west of the peninsula that the Church wanted to eradicate.

personas/cormac-mac-cuilennain/resumen.texto: King of Munster and bishop, based at Cashel, who died in the battle of Belach Mugna in 908. Tradition attributes to him the oldest version of Cormac's Glossary (Sanas Cormaic), although the surviving text has later additions.

personas/james-frazer/resumen.texto: Scottish anthropologist, author of The Golden Bough (1890), who gathered customs from around the world as remnants of a primitive fertility religion. He presented the Beltaine bonfires as remnants of human sacrifices and Samain as a Celtic festival of the dead; his comparative method, which assembled data without context, has been abandoned by anthropology, but his ideas still circulate.

personas/john-rhys/resumen.texto: First professor of Celtic languages at the University of Oxford (1877). In his Hibbert Lectures of 1886 and in Celtic Folklore (1901) he proposed that 1 November was the Celtic New Year, an idea he took from the Welsh and Manx folklore of the 19th century and which was later repeated as ancient fact.

personas/thomas-kendrick/resumen.texto: Archaeologist at the British Museum, of which he was director (1950-1959). His book The Druids (1927) was the first academic study to gather the ancient texts on the druids and separate them from the fantasies of the antiquaries.

personas/marie-louise-sjoestedt/resumen.texto: French Celticist, professor at the École pratique des hautes études. Her Dieux et héros des Celtes (1940) read Irish mythology as an ancient religious system with a method close to Dumézil's. She died in December 1940, at the age of forty, during the German occupation of Paris; the English translation of her book was published in 1949.

personas/jan-de-vries/resumen.texto: Dutch philologist of Leiden University, author of a handbook of Germanic religion and of Keltische Religion (1961), where he applied Dumézil's comparison to the Celts. He collaborated with the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands and was removed from the university after the war, which led to a review of the biases in his work.

personas/georges-dumezil/resumen.texto: French philologist who compared Indo-European mythologies and proposed that all of them express a “tripartite ideology”: religious and juridical sovereignty, warrior force and fertility. He applied the scheme to Caesar's druids, knights and common people, and to the Irish gods, and trained several Celticists. His theory was very influential and very disputed: Wouter Belier (1991) and others argue that the scheme is so elastic that it can be found in any society, and Arnaldo Momigliano and Carlo Ginzburg discussed the political ideology of his work from the 1930s, to which Dumézil replied.

personas/maire-macneill/resumen.texto: Irish folklorist of the Irish Folklore Commission. The Festival of Lughnasa (1962) gathered the customs of some two hundred gathering places in early August and proposed that they derived from a pre-Christian harvest festival dedicated to Lug.

personas/anne-ross/resumen.texto: British archaeologist and Celticist. Pagan Celtic Britain (1967) gathered the images and inscriptions of the gods of Britain and spread the idea of a “cult of the head” central to Celtic religion. With Don Robins she argued in 1989 that the Lindow Man was a sacrificed druid prince, a thesis that most specialists rejected.

personas/proinsias-mac-cana/resumen.texto: Irish Celticist of University College Dublin and the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies. In Celtic Mythology (1970) and other works he argued that medieval Irish literature preserves, beneath its Christian redaction, much of the pre-Christian oral tradition; he is one of the principal voices of the “nativist” position.

personas/christian-guyonvarch/resumen.texto: Breton Celticist and linguist, professor at Rennes. With his wife, Françoise Le Roux, he wrote Les Druides (The Druids) and other books that reconstruct Gaulish religion from Irish texts.

personas/francoise-le-roux/resumen.texto: French Celticist, a student of Dumézil, founder of the journal Ogam and co-author with Christian-J. Guyonvarc'h of Les Druides. Her method, which projects medieval Irish sources onto ancient Gaul, has been criticized by historians and archaeologists.

personas/jaan-puhvel/resumen.texto: Estonian-American linguist of the University of California, Los Angeles, a specialist in Hittite and comparative mythology; he had studied in Paris with Georges Dumézil. In Comparative Mythology (1987) he related the Irish mare rite recounted by Gerald of Wales to the Vedic horse sacrifice and to the Roman October Horse.

personas/martin-l-west/resumen.texto: British classical philologist of Oxford, editor of Hesiod and the Greek lyric poets. Indo-European Poetry and Myth (2007) is the broadest modern compendium of comparative Indo-European mythology and includes the Celtic data.

personas/richard-bradley/resumen.texto: British archaeologist of the University of Reading. The Passage of Arms (1990) showed that the deposition of weapons and metal objects in rivers, lakes and bogs was a continuous practice from the Neolithic and the Bronze Age to the Iron Age, and that it cannot be explained as chance losses.

personas/miranda-aldhouse-green/resumen.texto: British archaeologist, professor at Cardiff, who published as Miranda Green until 2000. She wrote the most widely used handbooks on Celtic gods and studies on human sacrifice, the bog bodies and the druids; she reads iconography and human remains as ritual evidence with more confidence than sceptical historians such as Ronald Hutton.

personas/ronald-hutton/resumen.texto: British historian of the University of Bristol, a specialist in ancient and modern paganism in the British Isles. He argues that very little is known with certainty about the pre-Christian religion of Britain and Ireland, and dismantled many supposed continuities, such as Samain as the Celtic New Year or the wise druid; some Celticists consider that he underrates what linguistic comparison and Irish literature allow us to reconstruct.

personas/jean-louis-brunaux/resumen.texto: French archaeologist of the CNRS who discovered the sanctuary of Gournay-sur-Aronde in 1975, excavated it until 1984, and then directed the excavation of Ribemont-sur-Ancre. He argued that the druids were an elite of philosophers influenced by Pythagoreanism through Massalia, and defended the reliability of Posidonius; he has been criticized for reading archaeology through the Greek texts.

personas/bernhard-maier/resumen.texto: German Celticist and historian of religions, professor at Tübingen. His Die Religion der Kelten (2001) and his dictionary of Celtic religion and culture carefully separate the ancient evidence from what is projected from the medieval Irish texts.

personas/john-carey-celtista/resumen.texto: American Celticist of University College Cork. He studied the Lebor Gabála Érenn as a “synthetic pseudohistory” produced by Christian scholars (1994) and the relation between Irish literature and ecclesiastical learning; he accepts that these texts preserve ancient materials, but asks that they be read first as medieval works.

hechos/ofrendas-en-aguas-de-la-edad-del-.texto: Offerings in rivers, lakes and bogs in the Bronze Age

Throughout north-western Europe swords, spears, shields and ornaments were thrown in during the Bronze Age, many of them deliberately broken, into rivers such as the Thames and the Seine, into lakes and into bogs, as at Flag Fen (England) or the Dowris deposit (Ireland). Richard Bradley showed that the practice begins in the Neolithic and continues into the Iron Age, at La Tène, Llyn Cerrig Bach or Tolosa: it predates everything that can be called Celtic. That the practice continued does not prove that the beliefs behind it were the same.

hechos/tumulos-neoliticos-reutilizados/r.texto: Beside the great Neolithic mound of Newgrange, built around 3200 BC, Roman coins, jewellery and gold from the 1st to 4th centuries were found, left as offerings by Iron Age Irish people or by visitors from Britain; the Mound of the Hostages at Tara, another Neolithic tomb, received new burials at the beginning of the Bronze Age. The medieval Irish texts make these mounds (síde) dwellings of the gods: for the Dindshenchas, Brú na Bóinne is the house of the Dagda and his son Óengus. The reuse shows a sustained respect for monuments two or three thousand years older, not that their builders were Celts.

hechos/carro-de-culto-de-strettweg/resum.texto: Bronze wagon found in 1851 in a princely Hallstatt tomb near Judenburg (Styria): on a platform with wheels, a tall female figure holds a bowl, surrounded by horsemen, warriors, deer and other figures, in a scene interpreted as a procession or a sacrifice. It is one of the few religious images of the Hallstatt period; whether the goddess is Celtic, from an earlier local religion, or an adaptation of Mediterranean models is debated.

hechos/herencia-indoeuropea-de-la-religi.texto: What comparison attributes to the Indo-European inheritance

Linguistics shows that the Celts inherited part of the Indo-European religious vocabulary: the word for “god”, such as Gaulish dēuos, Irish día, like Latin deus and Sanskrit deva, or the word for a sacred place, nemeton, related to Latin nemus, “grove”. The comparison of myths goes further and attributes to that inheritance a god of thunder (Taranis, compared with Thor and Perkunas), a father and ancestor god (Caesar's Gaulish Dis Pater, the Irish Dagda), the link between the horse and sovereignty, and the three functions of Dumézil reflected in the druids, the warriors and the common people. Each of these comparisons has been disputed: the Celtic texts are late and Christian, thematic similarities may be coincidental, and Dumézil's scheme is considered too elastic (Belier). What is solid is the kinship of the words; what is interpreted is the structure of the myths.

hechos/masalia-y-los-cultos-del-sur-de-l.texto: Massalia and the cults of southern Gaul

Strabo (IV.1.4-5) reports that the Massaliotes spread the cult of the Ephesian Artemis, and that the neighbouring Gauls learned from them to write their contracts in Greek. In Provence, the stone sculpture of Roquepertuse and Entremont follows Greek models, and the Gaulish inscriptions in Greek letters include religious dedications, such as that of Segomaros of Vaison, who offers a nemeton to the goddess Belesama. Brunaux argues that human images of the gods spread in Gaul through Greek and Roman influence, and that before this a cult without images had predominated.

hechos/dioses-de-los-galos-segun-cesar/t.texto: The gods of the Gauls according to Caesar

hechos/dioses-de-los-galos-segun-cesar/r.texto: Caesar (BG VI.17-18) says that the Gauls worship above all Mercury, the inventor of all arts, guide of the roads and protector of trade, of whom there are many images, and after him Apollo, Mars, Jupiter and Minerva; and that they all claim descent from Dis Pater, which is why they measure time by nights. It is an early example of what Tacitus will call interpretatio romana (Germania 43): Caesar gives the Roman names and not the Gaulish ones. It has been read as evidence of an orderly pantheon, with Lugus behind Mercury according to most scholars since Henri d'Arbois de Jubainville; but the gods of the inscriptions number in the hundreds and are very local, and Jane Webster and others see in the passage a Roman order imposed on scattered cults.

hechos/bardos-vates-y-druidas/titulo.texto: Bards, vates and druids according to Posidonius

hechos/bardos-vates-y-druidas/resumen.texto: Strabo (IV.4.4), Diodorus (V.31) and Ammianus Marcellinus (XV.9.8, who follows Timagenes) distinguish three classes of honoured men among the Gauls: the bards, poets who sing praises and satires to the lyre; the vates, diviners who interpret the sacrifices and study nature; and the druids, who deal with philosophy and judge lawsuits. Diodorus adds that no sacrifice is made without a philosopher, and that druids and bards stop armies on the point of battle. All three texts depend on Posidonius, who travelled through Gaul around 90 BC; the three words have parallels in Ireland (bard, fáith, druí) and in Wales, which suggests a real institution, although the division into three classes may be a Greek scheme.

hechos/primera-mencion-de-los-druidas/re.texto: According to Diogenes Laertius (3rd century AD, prologue 1 and 6), Sotion of Alexandria, around 200 BC, and a Magical treatise attributed to Aristotle already counted the druids of the Celts and the Galatians among the “barbarian philosophers”, alongside the Persian magi, the Chaldeans and the gymnosophists of India. It is the oldest mention of the name, and we know it only from a quotation of a quotation. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata I.15) repeats the list, and Hippolytus (Refutation I.25) makes the druids disciples of Pythagoras through the Thracian Zalmoxis: the image of the philosopher druid comes from this Alexandrian tradition.

hechos/los-druidas-segun-cesar/titulo.texto: The druids of Gaul according to Caesar

hechos/los-druidas-segun-cesar/resumen.texto: Caesar (BG VI.13-14) is the only one to describe the druids as an institution: together with the knights they form the two classes that count in Gaul; they direct the sacrifices, educate the young, judge disputes and crimes, and punish with exclusion from the sacrifices; they have a chief, elected sometimes by arms, and they meet once a year in a sacred place in the territory of the Carnutes, regarded as the centre of Gaul. They are exempt from war and taxes, learn for up to twenty years a great number of verses without committing them to writing, although they use Greek letters for other matters, and their doctrine is said to have originated in Britain. Caesar dealt with the Aeduan druid Diviciacus and knew Gaul at first hand, but he wrote for the Senate and for his career, and it is debated whether his portrait is a description or a Roman model, like a Gaulish college of pontiffs. Ronald Hutton observes that such powerful druids do not appear in the account of the conquest, and that the portrait served Caesar: wise so that Gaul would be worth the effort, organized so that they would be a threat, barbarians so that conquering them would be civilizing. Jane Webster (1999), by contrast, argues that what only Caesar reports—the annual assembly, arbitration between peoples, the British origin—is what one would expect of druids before the conquest, and that the anachronistic ones are those who copied Posidonius.

hechos/bosque-sagrado-de-masalia/titulo.texto: Caesar orders a sacred grove near Massalia to be felled

hechos/bosque-sagrado-de-masalia/resumen.texto: Lucan (Pharsalia III.399-452) describes a sacred grove near Massalia, so old that light had never entered it, with altars stained with human blood and crude images of the gods carved from tree trunks, which Caesar's soldiers did not dare to fell until he himself took up the axe. It is a poetic scene written a century later, but it agrees with other testimonies about sacred places: the Gaulish nemeton, which appears in place names (Nemetodurum, today Nanterre; Vernemetum in Britain; Nemetobriga in Gallaecia), and the Drunemeton, “sanctuary of oaks”, where the council of the Galatians met according to Strabo (XII.5.1). Archaeology, by contrast, finds mainly enclosures with ditches, such as Gournay.

hechos/inmortalidad-del-alma-segun-los-a.texto: The immortality of the soul according to the ancient authors

Almost all ancient authors attribute to the druids the teaching that the soul does not die: Caesar (BG VI.14) says that it passes from one body to another and that for this reason the Gauls do not fear death; Diodorus (V.28) compares it with the doctrine of Pythagoras and reports that at funerals they throw letters addressed to the dead into the fire; Mela (III.19) and Valerius Maximus (II.6.10) add that they lent money to be repaid in the other world, and Lucan (I.454-458) that for them death is the midpoint of a long life. Tombs with food, weapons and chariots are compatible with belief in another life. It is debated whether the Gauls believed in reincarnation, with Pythagorean influence through Massalia (Brunaux), or whether “metempsychosis” is a Greek reading of a belief in the other world (Hutton, Maier). Maier points out that transmigration appears only in authors who depend on Posidonius, and that the Pythagoreans did not eat meat, whereas the Gauls sacrificed and ate animals. The medieval Irish texts, such as the Voyage of Bran, describe instead an other world of islands and mounds that one reaches while still alive, not a rebirth in another body.

hechos/rito-del-muerdago/titulo.texto: The mistletoe rite according to Pliny

hechos/rito-del-muerdago/resumen.texto: Pliny the Elder (Natural History XVI.249-251) reports that the druids have nothing more sacred than mistletoe and the oak on which it grows, and that on the sixth day of the moon a priest dressed in white climbs the tree, cuts the mistletoe with a golden sickle and receives it in a white cloak, before sacrificing two white bulls; they call it “the all-healing” and believe it gives fertility to barren animals and serves against poisons. In another book (XXIV.103-104) he describes how the druids gathered the herbs selago and samolus, without iron, dressed in white and barefoot or fasting. It is the only testimony to these rites, written in Rome more than a century after the conquest, and Pliny does not say where he took it from; Bernhard Maier observes that the “golden sickle” would more likely have been gilded bronze, and that the essential point was to avoid iron. It became the most repeated scene in the modern image of the druid.

hechos/huevo-de-serpiente/titulo.texto: The serpent egg and the Vocontian knight

hechos/huevo-de-serpiente/resumen.texto: Pliny (XXIX.52-54) describes the anguinum, an “egg” formed by the saliva of intertwined snakes, which the druids gathered at a particular phase of the moon and which gave an advantage in lawsuits, and says he saw one. He reports that the emperor Claudius had a Roman knight from the Gaulish people of the Vocontii put to death because he was carrying one during a trial. It is one of the few concrete cases of the application of the prohibition of druidism, and it shows that Rome persecuted it as magic.

hechos/prohibicion-del-druidismo/resumen.texto: According to Suetonius (Claudius 25.5), Augustus prohibited the religion of the druids for Roman citizens, as “of atrocious cruelty”, and Claudius abolished it completely; Pliny (XXX.13) attributes the suppression to a decree of the Senate under Tiberius, and Aurelius Victor again to Claudius. Roman authors present it as the end of human sacrifice (Strabo IV.4.5), and modern historiography has explained it in this way; Jane Webster and others argue that the motive was political, because the druids formed a network of authority above the peoples and could lead resistance. They did not disappear all at once: Mela speaks of secret teachings in caves and forests, Tacitus shows them on Mona in the year 60 and in Gaul in 69, and in the 4th century there were still families who claimed to be descended from druids.

hechos/profecia-druidica-del-incendio-de.texto: The druids announce the end of Roman rule

Tacitus (Histories IV.54) reports that, when the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol burned during the civil war of 69, the druids proclaimed with “vain superstition” that it was a sign of the wrath of the gods, and that rule over the world would pass to the peoples beyond the Alps. It coincided with the revolt of the Batavians under Civilis and with the “empire of the Gauls” of Classicus and Tutor. It is the last testimony to the druids as political actors and the basis of Webster's reading, which sees them as guides of a resistance movement.

hechos/mujeres-y-religion-en-las-fuentes.texto: Priestesses, seers and sorceresses in the ancient sources

The ancient sources do not speak of female druids before the 3rd century, but they do speak of women with religious functions: Strabo (IV.4.6, following Posidonius) describes the women of the Samnites, who lived without men on an island facing the mouth of the Loire and served a god whom he identifies with Dionysus; Mela (III.48), nine virgin priestesses of the island of Sena who calmed the sea and foretold the future; Tacitus (Annals XIV.30), women dressed in black with torches among the druids of Mona; Plutarch, Camma, priestess of Artemis in Galatia. The Historia Augusta speaks of seer “druidesses” in the 3rd century, and the lead tablet from Larzac of a group of sorceresses. Romanticism and some currents of the 20th century built on these data druid priestesses and a Celtic matriarchy that the sources do not support; what they do show is that there were women with religious and magical authority.

hechos/profesores-de-burdeos-de-linaje-d.texto: Teachers of Bordeaux who descended from druids

Ausonius, in his poem on the professors of Bordeaux (around 380-390), says that the rhetorician Attius Patera was of druidic stock among the Bayocasses, “if fame does not deceive”, and that his family came from the temple of Belenus; and that the grammarian Phoebicius, keeper of the temple of Belenus, was of a druidic lineage from Armorica. It shows that in the Christian Gaul of the 4th century, descent from druids was a mark of prestige in educated families, and that the cult of Belenus had had hereditary servants; it does not prove that there were still druids in office.

hechos/druidas-en-la-irlanda-cristiana/t.texto: The druids in the Christian Irish texts

hechos/druidas-en-la-irlanda-cristiana/r.texto: In Ireland the druí appears in Christian texts as a magician and diviner of kings: in Muirchú's Life of Patrick (late 7th century), the druids of King Lóegaire of Tara confront Patrick when he lights the Easter fire on the hill of Slane, and lose a contest of miracles; Adomnán reports that Columba defeated the magician Broichan at the court of the Pictish king Bridei; the Lorica of Patrick asks for protection against their spells, and the laws of the 7th and 8th centuries give them a lower rank than that of the poets. These are accounts of Christian victory written two centuries after the events, but they show that the word was still alive and that the filid, the learned poets, inherited much of their prestige. That these Irish druids were the same as Caesar's Gauls is an assumption that McCone and Hutton criticize.

hechos/el-druida-sabio-invencion-moderna.texto: The wise druid, a modern invention

From the 17th century, antiquaries such as John Aubrey and William Stukeley (1740) attributed Stonehenge and Avebury to the druids, whom they imagined as priests of a patriarchal and almost monotheistic religion, close to Christianity. Romanticism made them patriotic bards, philosophers of nature and victims of Rome, and from this came Iolo Morganwg's Gorsedd (1792) and neo-druidism. The megaliths are some two thousand years older than the first documented druids; Kendrick (1927), Piggott (1968) and Hutton (2009) reconstructed how that image was formed, from Pliny, the Alexandrian tradition and the imagination of each era.

hechos/acusaciones-de-sacrificio-humano/.texto: Ancient authors accuse the Gauls of sacrificing men

Several Greek and Roman authors claim that the Gauls sacrificed men: Caesar (BG VI.16) speaks of huge wicker figures filled with living men, which were set on fire, preferably with thieves, and with innocent people if there were not enough; Diodorus (V.31-32) and Strabo (IV.4.5), following Posidonius, speak of divining by the convulsions of a stabbed man, and of criminals impaled after five years of waiting; Cicero (Pro Fonteio 31) accuses the Gaulish witnesses of staining their altars with human blood.
