These authors had an interest in showing the Gauls as barbarians—Cicero was defending a governor accused by them, and Caesar justified his conquest—and the Romans themselves buried Gauls alive in the Forum Boarium; Bruce Lincoln (1988) replies that the accounts cannot be mere Roman propaganda, because they come from Greek authors, such as Posidonius, who predate the conquest. Archaeology confirms violent deaths and ritual handling of corpses at some sites, but not the wicker figures or the scale suggested by the texts. Miranda Aldhouse-Green accepts sacrifice as a real practice, though rarer than the Romans say and typical of moments of crisis; Ronald Hutton stresses that no archaeological case is indisputable.

hechos/galos-enterrados-vivos-en-el-foro.texto: Rome buries alive two Gauls and two Greeks

After the defeat at Cannae, according to Livy (XXII.57), the Romans buried alive in the Forum Boarium a Gaulish man and a Gaulish woman and a Greek man and a Greek woman, on the instruction of the Sibylline Books, in a rite that Livy calls “very un-Roman”; Plutarch (Marcellus 3) reports the same for 228 BC, and there was another case in 114-113 BC. It is a Roman human sacrifice directed against the Gauls, and it shows that the Romans, who accused other peoples of this practice, also practised it.

hechos/santuario-de-gournay/resumen.texto: Sanctuary of the Bellovaci excavated by Jean-Louis Brunaux, Patrice Méniel and André Rapin between 1975 and 1984: a square enclosure with a ditch and palisade, in whose centre there were pits where the bodies of old sacrificed oxen were left to rot, while the meat of pigs and lambs was eaten at feasts. In the ditch some two thousand weapons came to light, many bent or broken on purpose, and human bones, above all skulls with cut marks, which Brunaux interprets as war trophies displayed at the entrance. It is the best archaeological evidence of an organized pre-Roman Gaulish cult, and what it shows—animal sacrifices, the display of trophies—agrees only in part with what the texts report.

hechos/santuario-de-ribemont/resumen.texto: At Ribemont-sur-Ancre, where Jean-Louis Cadoux's team found the Gaulish ditch beneath the Roman sanctuary in 1982, more than 40,000 Iron Age human bones came to light, from several hundred people, almost all young men and without any skulls, together with thousands of weapons, and square structures made of long human bones piled up around a well containing burnt remains. Brunaux, who at first read it as evidence of the human sacrifices of Caesar and Diodorus, later interpreted it as a trophy erected around 260 BC with the bodies of enemies killed in a battle, exhibited and beheaded, and on the basis of the coins he attributed the victory to the Ambiani over a people of the Lisieux region; the British archaeologist Martin Brown proposed that it was a memorial to one's own dead, and others read it as a sacrifice. It shows a ritual treatment of war dead that agrees with what Posidonius reports about heads, but it does not prove sacrifices of living people. A Gallo-Roman sanctuary was later built on the site.

hechos/hombre-de-lindow/resumen.texto: Body of a man of about twenty-five, found by peat cutters on 1 August 1984 at Lindow Moss (Cheshire), who died between 2 BC and AD 119 according to radiocarbon dates that gave discordant results. He had blows to the head, a cord of sinew around his neck and a cut in his throat, and in his stomach there were remains of toasted bread and some grains of mistletoe pollen. Anne Ross and Don Robins took him for a sacrificed druid prince, killed in a triple death for three gods; Robert Connolly, Stephen Briggs and Jody Joy (2009) pointed out that some of the wounds may have been inflicted after death and that the cord may have been an ornament, and Ronald Hutton that if he died after the Romans reached northern England, in the 60s, a sacrifice would be less likely. That it was a violent death is certain; that it was a sacrifice, and even less a druidic one, is interpretation.

hechos/hombres-de-old-croghan-y-clonycav.texto: The men of Old Croghan and Clonycavan

Two Iron Age bodies found in Irish bogs in 2003. The Clonycavan man (Meath), who died between 392 and 201 BC, received several blows to the head and face and had his hair raised with vegetable oil and a pine resin imported from south-western France or northern Spain; the Old Croghan man (Offaly), who died between 362 and 175 BC, a very tall man, was stabbed, cut at the neck and the waist, and had deep cuts beneath the nipples. Eamonn Kelly interprets them as kings or rivals sacrificed at the boundaries of kingdoms, in a rite linked to sovereignty, and the cuts on the nipples as the mark of a rejected king; others think of damage to the bog, torture, or sacrifices for the harvest. It is a hypothesis that joins archaeological finds with medieval texts and has no direct proof.

hechos/cabezas-cortadas-segun-posidonio/.texto: Diodorus (V.29) and Strabo (IV.4.5), following Posidonius, report that the Gauls cut off the heads of slain enemies, hung them from the necks of their horses and nailed them at the entrance of their houses, and that they kept those of the most noble in cedar oil and would not return them even for their weight in gold; Posidonius says he saw this many times and ended up getting used to it. Livy tells the same of the Gallic horsemen who, in 295 BC, before Sentinum, annihilated a legion near Clusium (X.26), and of the skull of the consul Postumius turned into a cup (XXIII.24); the nailed skulls of Entremont and the niches of Roquepertuse confirm it in southern Gaul. Anne Ross made the head the centre of Celtic religion, a “cult of the head”; Hutton and others prefer to speak of a warlike practice of trophies, shared with other peoples, whose religious meaning we do not know.

hechos/estatuas-de-entremont/titulo.texto: The statues of seated warriors with severed heads from Entremont

hechos/estatuas-de-entremont/resumen.texto: In the oppidum of the Salyes at Entremont, near Aix-en-Provence, inhabited from 180-170 BC and destroyed by the Romans around 124-123 BC, excavations in the 1940s brought to light stone statues of seated warriors with a hand resting on severed heads, a pillar with carved heads and human skulls with nail holes. It is the clearest archaeological confirmation of the trophy heads described by Posidonius. It is debated whether the statues represent heroes or ancestors of the elite, and whether the complex was a sanctuary or a place of political assembly.

hechos/muertos-sentados-de-acy-romance/r.texto: At the Gaulish settlement of Acy-Romance (Ardennes), excavated by Bernard Lambot, the bodies of some twenty young men were found buried seated in narrow pits, dating from the early 1st century BC, near a building interpreted as a temple. Lambot proposes that they were sacrificed and dried out before burial; others think of a funerary rite reserved for certain people. It is one of the most cited cases in the debate on human sacrifice in Gaul.

hechos/recintos-cuadrangulares/resumen.texto: Square enclosures with a ditch and embankment from the end of the Iron Age, very numerous in southern Germany and present in France and Bohemia. Since the excavations at Holzhausen (Bavaria), with deep wells, they were interpreted as sanctuaries, and in a well of the Fellbach-Schmiden enclosure wooden animal figures came to light, dated by dendrochronology to around 123 BC. Later excavations found houses, granaries and agricultural work at many of them, and today they are seen as farms or elite centres that also had ritual functions: an example of how the reading of the “sacred” in Celtic archaeology has changed.

hechos/cabeza-de-msecke-zehrovice/resume.texto: Male stone head with a torc, moustache and protruding eyes, dated 150-50 BC, found in 1943 in a double square enclosure northwest of Prague. It is one of the few large Celtic sculptures of the human figure; it is debated whether it represents a god, a hero or an ancestor, and the fact that it appeared in an enclosure that may also have been a farm shows how uncertain a religious reading of such places is.

hechos/oro-de-tolosa/resumen.texto: In 106 BC the consul Quintus Servilius Caepio took Tolosa, city of the Volcae Tectosages, and seized an enormous treasure kept in sacred enclosures and in lakes; much of it disappeared on the way to Massalia, and Caepio was tried for stealing it. Strabo (IV.1.13), following Posidonius, says that the gold did not come from the plunder of Delphi, as was told, but was native to the country, and that the Gauls consecrated it to the gods by throwing it into lakes; the Romans who later bought those lakes extracted silver from them in bars shaped like millstones. It is the clearest ancient testimony to offerings in water; the legend of the gold of Tolosa that brought misfortune to whoever touched it, recorded by Justin (XXXII.3), originates in this episode.

hechos/ofrendas-de-llyn-cerrig-bach/resu.texto: In 1942, while cutting peat for the runway of the Valley air base on Anglesey, metal objects came to light (181 are known today): swords, spears, shields, chariot and harness fittings, cauldrons, a trumpet, blacksmith's tools, iron bars and two neck chains for slaves, together with animal bones. Many had been deliberately broken, and several came from southern England and some from Ireland. Cyril Fox (1946) interpreted them as offerings and linked them to the druids of Mona whom Suetonius Paulinus attacked in the year 60, according to Tacitus (Annals XIV.30). Later reviews see them as successive offerings, deposited between 300 BC and AD 100, rather than as a single assemblage: the votive reading is accepted, the link to the druids is a hypothesis.

hechos/caldero-de-gundestrup/resumen.texto: Silver cauldron 69 centimetres in diameter, found dismantled in 1891 in a bog in Himmerland (Denmark), dated between 150 BC and the turn of the era. Its plates show a figure with antlers seated cross-legged, with a torc and a ram-headed serpent—the image identified with Cernunnos—a god with a wheel, a giant figure dipping a man into a vat in front of a row of warriors, the sacrifice of a bull, and animals such as elephants and griffins. On the basis of the silverwork, Bergquist and Taylor (1987) argue that Thracian goldsmiths made it, perhaps commissioned by the Scordisci, and that it reached the north with the Cimbri; Garrett Olmsted attributes it to workshops in north-western Gaul because of its resemblance to Armorican coins, and reads scenes from the Irish Táin in its plates. It was deposited dismantled and stacked, perhaps as an offering, far from the Celtic world (studies disagree on whether the site was then a bog or dry land); it is at once the most cited image of Celtic religion and one of the most disputed.

hechos/altar-de-las-tres-galias/titulo.texto: Altar of Rome and Augustus at Lugdunum

hechos/altar-de-las-tres-galias/lugar.texto: Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls, Lyon

hechos/altar-de-las-tres-galias/resumen.texto: On 1 August 12 BC, Drusus inaugurated at Lugdunum the altar of Rome and Augustus, where the delegates of the sixty peoples of the Three Gauls met each year in a council and chose a Gaulish priest for the imperial cult (Strabo IV.3.2). It was the Roman way of giving the Gaulish nobility a common and loyal cult, in place of the druidic assembly of the Carnutes described by Caesar. Some scholars see in the date the continuation of a Gaulish festival of Lugus, whose name the city bears, equivalent to the Irish Lughnasa; others point out that 1 August was the anniversary of Augustus's capture of Alexandria and that there is no evidence of a Gaulish festival on that day.

hechos/pilar-de-los-nautas/titulo.texto: The Pillar of the Boatmen of Paris

hechos/pilar-de-los-nautas/resumen.texto: Votive column dedicated to Jupiter by the boatmen of the Parisii people in the time of Tiberius, found in 1711 under the choir of Notre-Dame, where it had been reused in the 4th-century wall. Its reliefs show Roman gods alongside Gaulish gods with their names in Latin: Esus cutting a tree, Tarvos Trigaranus (a bull with three cranes), Cernunnos, an old man with antlers from which torcs hang, and Smertrios. It is the only undisputed attestation of the name Cernunnos, although the stone is now damaged (the C is missing) and the reading depends on the copy published when it was found; it is also one of the first monuments in which Gaulish gods appear with image and name, already in a Roman form. The myth of Esus, the bull and the cranes, repeated in a relief from Trier dedicated to Mercury, is not known from any text. Apart from the pillar, Esus has only one secure inscription, on the base of a statuette found in Carinthia in 1987.

hechos/ogmios-segun-luciano/titulo.texto: Ogmios, the Gaulish Heracles according to Lucian

hechos/ogmios-segun-luciano/resumen.texto: Lucian of Samosata tells in his Heracles, around 175, that he saw in Gaul a painting of Heracles, whom the Gauls called Ogmios, as an almost bald old man with weathered skin who drags along a contented crowd, bound by the ears with fine chains of gold and amber that come out of his tongue; a Gaul who spoke Greek explained to him that for them the strength of Heracles was eloquence, which reaches its full power in old age. Apart from Lucian, the name appears only on two curse tablets from Brigantium (Bregenz, Austria), and no similar image has been found. It has been linked with Ogma, the Irish god to whom tradition attributes the invention of ogham, but that etymology has problems of chronology and phonetics, and the text is a rhetorical piece with which Lucian, already old, defended his own ability to speak in public.

hechos/epona-en-roma/titulo.texto: Epona, goddess of horsemen, in Rome

hechos/epona-en-roma/resumen.texto: Inscriptions from the equites singulares, the emperor's mounted guard recruited in the Rhine and Danube provinces, show the cult of Epona in Rome itself in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, and a rural calendar from Italy set her festival for 18 December. Apuleius (Metamorphoses III.27) describes an image of her crowned with roses in a stable. It is the clearest case of a goddess of Celtic origin adopted by the Roman army and spread throughout the Empire, although not the only one with dedications in Rome: Belenus has them too.

hechos/culto-de-las-matronas-en-el-rin/t.texto: The cult of the Matronae on the Lower Rhine

hechos/culto-de-las-matronas-en-el-rin/r.texto: In the surroundings of Cologne, Bonn and Jülich, hundreds of altars to triads of mother goddesses were erected in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, such as the Matronae Aufaniae of Bonn or the Vacallinehae of the sanctuary at Pesch, in the Eifel. The devotees were soldiers, officials and families of the Ubii, a Germanic people settled on the Roman bank of the Rhine, and the goddesses' epithets are both Celtic and Germanic. It is the clearest example that “Celtic” cults of the Roman period mixed traditions of different peoples in a Roman form.

hechos/columnas-de-jupiter-y-el-gigante/.texto: In the provinces of Germania and eastern Gaul, hundreds of columns were erected, crowned by a mounted Jupiter who strikes down a giant with serpent legs, on a base with four Roman gods; the great Jupiter column of Mainz, from the 1st century, is its Roman antecedent. It is debated whether the celestial rider and the shaft decorated like a tree express, in a Roman form, a Celtic sky or thunder god, such as Taranis (Green, de Vries), or whether they are a provincial creation with no demonstrable Celtic root.

hechos/beleno-defiende-aquilea/titulo.texto: The defenders of Aquileia invoke Belenus

hechos/beleno-defiende-aquilea/resumen.texto: When the emperor Maximinus Thrax besieged Aquileia in 238, the city held out and Maximinus was killed by his own soldiers. Herodian (VIII.3) reports that the defenders said they had seen Belenus, the patron of the city, whom they identified with Apollo, fighting for them in the air. The numerous inscriptions from Aquileia confirm that a god of Celtic origin was the main civic deity of a great Roman city.

hechos/samain/resumen.texto: Irish festival of 1 November that marked the beginning of winter. In medieval texts it is the time of the great royal assemblies, such as the feast of Tara, of the payment of tributes and of many deaths of kings and heroes, and the night on which the otherworld of the síde is open; its name is compared with the month Samonios of the Coligny calendar. The idea of Samain as the “Celtic New Year” and “festival of the dead” was formulated by John Rhŷs and James Frazer at the end of the 19th century on the basis of modern Welsh, Manx and Irish customs; Ronald Hutton, who does not doubt that there was a great pagan festival in early November, argues that there is no ancient evidence for either. As for Halloween, what is documented is that bonfires, divination and costumes on the eve of November are recorded in Scotland and Ireland from the 16th to the 18th centuries, and that emigrants took them to America. For the date of All Saints, celebrated on 1 November in Ireland and in Northumbria around 800, Frazer assumed a Celtic origin and Hutton argues for a Germanic and Roman one; others point to Irish influence on the church of Northumbria.

hechos/imbolc-y-brigida/titulo.texto: Imbolc and the feast of Brigid

hechos/imbolc-y-brigida/resumen.texto: On 1 February, Imbolc or Oímelc, is in Irish texts one of the four festivals of the year, linked to the milk of ewes according to Cormac's Glossary, and it is the day of Saint Brigid, abbess of Kildare, who died around 525. The Glossary also speaks of a Brigit who was a poet and goddess, daughter of the Dagda, with two sisters of the same name, a physician and a smith; Gerald of Wales (around 1188) reports that nineteen nuns kept a perpetual fire at Kildare, which the archbishop of Dublin ordered extinguished in 1220, was relit, and burned until the Reformation, and that the Brigidine sisters relit it in 1993. Those who see in the saint a Christianized goddess rely on the name, the date, the miracles of abundance and the fire; sceptics, such as Hutton, reply that the goddess appears only in a 10th-century glossary and the fire only in a 12th-century text.

hechos/beltaine/resumen.texto: Festival of 1 May that in Ireland and Scotland marked the beginning of summer and the moving of cattle to the high pastures. Cormac's Glossary (around 900) says that on that day the druids lit two fires with incantations and made the cattle pass between them to protect them from disease, and the tradition recorded by Geoffrey Keating in the 17th century places the great Beltaine fire at Uisneach; May bonfires continued in the Scottish and Irish countryside until the 19th century. Frazer read them as remnants of human sacrifices, without evidence; the link between its name and the god Belenus is possible but disputed.

hechos/lugnasad/titulo.texto: Lughnasa and the fair of Tailtiu

hechos/lugnasad/resumen.texto: Festival of 1 August, the beginning of the harvest, named after the god Lug: according to the Book of Invasions (Lebor Gabála) and the Dindshenchas, Lug instituted the fair of Tailtiu in honour of his foster mother, who died of exhaustion after clearing a plain for cultivation. The fair, with games, horse races and marriage agreements, was presided over by the kings of Tara, and the annals record it until the 12th century. Máire MacNeill (1962) gathered the hill climbs and first-fruit offerings of late July that survived into the 20th century—the best known, the pilgrimage to Croagh Patrick—and proposed that they came from a pre-Christian festival of Lug; that the date coincides with that of the altar at Lugdunum is read by some as a shared inheritance and by others as coincidence.

hechos/debate-nativista-y-antinativista/.texto: The debate between nativists and anti-nativists

During the 20th century it was debated how much of the pre-Christian religion the Irish texts written by monks preserve. The “nativists”—Marie-Louise Sjoestedt; Kenneth Jackson, who in 1964 called the Táin “a window onto the Iron Age”; Proinsias Mac Cana—hold that this literature transmits, with Christian touches, a very ancient oral tradition. From James Carney (1955) and above all Kim McCone (1990), the “anti-nativists” read it as the creation of Christian scholars who used the Bible, the classics and ecclesiastical history to construct a past; John Carey and Ronald Hutton share much of this criticism. Today most accept both things: there are ancient materials, but they arrive transformed, and each text is first read in its medieval context.

hechos/leyes-de-teodosio-contra-el-pagan.texto: The laws of Theodosius I of 391 and 392, preserved in the Theodosian Code (XVI.10), prohibited sacrifices, access to temples and all pagan worship in the Empire, including domestic worship. In Gaul and Britain they also reached the cults of gods of Celtic origin with Roman names. Archaeology shows that many rural sanctuaries remained in use for some decades more and that their abandonment was gradual and uneven.

hechos/martin-destruye-santuarios/titulo.texto: Martin of Tours destroys temples and sacred trees

hechos/martin-destruye-santuarios/resume.texto: According to Sulpicius Severus (Life of Saint Martin 12-15), the bishop Martin toured the countryside of central Gaul destroying rural temples and raising churches or monasteries in their place: he had a sacred pine beside a temple felled while pagans challenged him to stand beneath it, he halted with the sign of the cross a procession that he took for a pagan procession of peasants carrying images through the fields and which turned out to be a funeral, and he faced crowds defending their sanctuaries among the Aedui. It is hagiography, written to make Martin a model bishop, and it is not known how much is exaggeration; but it is the only contemporary account of the end of rural cults in Gaul, and it shows that this end was the work of bishops and monks who used force, not only laws.

hechos/concilios-contra-los-cultos-rural.texto: The Gaulish councils condemn the cult of stones, trees and springs

From the 5th century, the councils of Gaul (Arles, Tours in 567, Auxerre at the end of the 6th century) and the sermons of Caesarius of Arles condemn Christians who light torches, make vows or eat beside trees, springs and stones, and who on the Kalends of January disguise themselves as animals. They show that open-air practices remained alive long after the legal prohibition. Whether these were remnants of Gaulish religion, of rural Roman religion or customs with no belief behind them, and how much of these texts is a repeated formula, is debated.

hechos/martin-de-braga-contra-los-cultos.texto: Martin of Braga preaches against the rural cults of Gallaecia

Around 572, after the second council of Braga, the bishop Martin wrote a sermon for the peasants of Gallaecia that condemns lighting candles beside stones, trees, springs and crossroads, throwing bread into springs, and venerating nymphs, lamiae and Neptune. Galician Celticism saw in it a living Celtic religion; historians point out that it uses Roman names and partly follows Caesarius of Arles, so that it shows persistent rural practices but does not allow them to be attributed to a Celtic origin.

hechos/ofrendas-al-lago-del-gevaudan/tit.texto: Offerings to the lake of Gévaudan

hechos/ofrendas-al-lago-del-gevaudan/res.texto: Gregory of Tours tells that in his time the peasants of the Gévaudan gathered each year beside a lake on Mount Helanus and for three days threw into it clothes, linen, cheese, wax and bread, and ate and drank, until a bishop raised a church beside the lake and persuaded them to bring the offerings to it instead. The lake is identified with that of Saint-Andéol, on the Aubrac, to which pilgrimages continued until the 19th century. It is one of the clearest examples of how the Church Christianized a practice of offerings in water with prehistoric roots, without our knowing which god they were directed to.

hechos/yegua-de-tir-conaill/titulo.texto: The mare rite of Tír Conaill according to Gerald

hechos/yegua-de-tir-conaill/resumen.texto: Gerald of Wales tells in the Topography of Ireland that in Tír Conaill, in the north of Ireland, the new king publicly coupled with a white mare, which was then sacrificed and boiled, and the king bathed in the broth and ate and drank it with his people. Jaan Puhvel and other comparativists relate it to the Vedic aśvamedha, in which the queen symbolically lay down with the sacrificed horse, and to the October Horse of Rome, as remnants of an Indo-European rite that linked kingship with the horse; along this line Epona, the Irish Macha and the Welsh Rhiannon are also read. But the account is unique and was written by a cleric who wanted to show the Irish as barbarians to justify the conquest, and many historians consider it slander or rumour: the comparison is suggestive but rests on a single hostile testimony.

hechos/pozos-santos/titulo.texto: The holy wells of Ireland and Britain

hechos/pozos-santos/resumen.texto: In Ireland some three thousand holy wells are recorded, almost all dedicated to saints, to which pilgrims went on fixed dates to be cured, to walk around them sunwise and to leave ribbons, coins or pins; similar customs existed in Wales, Scotland, Cornwall and Brittany. They have often been presented as pagan sanctuaries of the waters, Christianized and in continuity with sacred springs such as those of Coventina or Sequana. Hutton and others note that almost no well has evidence of worship predating Christianity, and that many of its customs are documented only from the 17th century: the continuity of offerings in water is proven as a practice, not that of each place or of its beliefs.

lugares/gournay-sur-aronde/resumen.texto: Sanctuary of the Bellovaci in northern Gaul, discovered by Jean-Louis Brunaux in 1975 and excavated until 1984: a square enclosure with a ditch and palisade, in use from the 4th century BC, where weapons, ox skulls and human remains were displayed. It was burned and levelled at the end of the 1st century BC, and in the 4th century AD a Gallo-Roman temple was built on the same spot.

lugares/ribemont-sur-ancre/resumen.texto: Site in the Somme valley where, above a large deposit of Iron Age human bones, a Gallo-Roman sanctuary with a temple, a theatre and baths was later built. Roger Agache discovered it through aerial photography in 1962, and the Roman sanctuary was excavated from the end of that decade; in 1982 the Gaulish ditch was found underneath, and the excavation of the Gaulish sanctuary was later directed by Jean-Louis Brunaux.

lugares/roquepertuse/resumen.texto: Fortified settlement in Provence, near Velaux, with a stone portico containing niches for human skulls, a stone bird, a double head and statues of seated warriors with their legs crossed. Henri de Gérin-Ricard excavated it in 1917-1927 and interpreted it as a sanctuary of the Celto-Ligurians on the eve of the Roman conquest; the excavations of 1989-2002, directed by Philippe Boissinot, showed that in the 3rd century BC it was a village with an oppidum and houses on terraces, which suffered a violent destruction in that century and was abandoned at the beginning of the 2nd, decades before Rome arrived. The statues, which some date by their clothing to the 6th or 5th century BC, may have been reused, and their original use is unclear.

lugares/fuentes-del-sena/nombre.texto: Sanctuary of the Source of the Seine

lugares/fuentes-del-sena/resumen.texto: Gallo-Roman sanctuary of the goddess Sequana beside the source of the Seine, at Saint-Germain-Source-Seine (Burgundy), with a temple, porticoes and pools. Henri Corot found there in 1933 a bronze statuette of the goddess standing in a boat with a duck-shaped prow and, in the excavations of 1963, some two hundred wooden ex-votos preserved in the mud, part of a total of about 1,500 ex-votos, representing bodies, heads, limbs and organs of the pilgrims who sought healing.

lugares/templo-de-mercurio-del-puy-de-do.texto: Temple of Mercury on the Puy de Dôme

Gallo-Roman temple on the summit of the Puy de Dôme volcano, in Arvernian territory, rebuilt in the 2nd century on a larger scale to receive pilgrims. An inscription dedicates it to Mercury Dumias, a Mercury with a local epithet; it is debated whether this is the site of the colossal Mercury that, according to Pliny (XXXIV.45), the sculptor Zenodorus made for the Arverni.

lugares/coligny/resumen.texto: Village in the Ain department, near Lyon, where in 1897 the fragments of the bronze Gaulish calendar that bears its name were found, together with remains of a bronze statue of a naked god with a spear, probably Mars.

lugares/lac-de-saint-andeol/resumen.texto: Glacial lake on the Aubrac plateau (Lozère) that is usually identified with the lake of Mount Helanus, where, according to Gregory of Tours, the peasants of the Gévaudan threw offerings every year.

lugares/aquae-sulis/resumen.texto: Roman sanctuary and baths built around the year 60 over the hot spring of Bath, dedicated to Sulis Minerva: it joined a British goddess of the spring with the Roman Minerva. Solinus (3rd century) reports that in her temple a perpetual fire burned that did not turn to ash but to stone, perhaps coal. Thousands of coins and some 130 curse tablets have come out of the spring.

lugares/lydney-park/nombre.texto: Temple of Nodens at Lydney Park

lugares/lydney-park/resumen.texto: Roman healing sanctuary dedicated to Nodens above the River Severn, with a temple, a guest house, baths and a portico interpreted as a place of ritual dreaming. Mortimer and Tessa Wheeler excavated it in 1928-1929; the Wheelers dated it to after 364, but later reviews move it back to the 3rd century, although the chronology remains disputed. Figurines of dogs and the curse tablet of Silvianus were found there.

lugares/pozo-de-coventina/resumen.texto: Sacred spring beside the fort of Brocolitia (Carrawburgh), on Hadrian's Wall, dedicated to the goddess Coventina, who is known with certainty only from the inscriptions of this site (at least ten). Excavated by John Clayton in 1876, it yielded 13,487 coins, from Mark Antony to Gratian, altars, a relief of three nymphs, incense burners and hairpins thrown in as offerings. The coins and the stones that covered the well indicate an abrupt end around 388, perhaps because of the laws of Theodosius against paganism.

lugares/llyn-cerrig-bach/resumen.texto: Small lake in western Anglesey (Mona) where, in 1942, during the construction of the Valley air base, 181 Iron Age metal objects came to light; they had been thrown into the water as offerings between 300 BC and AD 100.

lugares/lindow-moss/resumen.texto: Peat bog near Wilmslow (Cheshire) where, in 1983 and 1984, the remains of several Iron Age or Roman-period bodies were found, among them the Lindow Man.

lugares/flag-fen/resumen.texto: Bronze Age wooden causeway crossing a marsh near Peterborough, built from about 1300 BC. For centuries, swords, daggers, ornaments and tools, many of them deliberately broken, were thrown in alongside it: it is one of the best examples of offerings in water before the Iron Age.

lugares/tlachtga/resumen.texto: Hill in County Meath crowned by a four-ring earthwork enclosure. The tradition recorded by Keating in the 17th century makes it the place of the Samhain fire lit by the druids; recent excavations, published from 2016 onward, showed ritual use with feasts and large fires from the Bronze Age to the end of the Iron Age, but these cannot be dated to Samhain. Since the late 1990s neopagan groups have celebrated Samhain there.

lugares/teltown/resumen.texto: Site in County Meath where the Óenach Tailten was held, the great fair with games, horse races and marriage agreements that Irish literature attributes to Lug and places at Lughnasa. The Irish annals mention it until the 12th century.

lugares/penalba-de-villastar/resumen.texto: Rock face 1.5 kilometres long near Teruel, on the eastern edge of Celtiberia, with hundreds of inscriptions and carvings, discovered by Juan Cabré in 1910. It is interpreted as a Celtiberian rock sanctuary, perhaps dedicated to Lugus.
